bib.title: Number Cookbook: Number Understanding of Language Models and How to Improve It

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Number Cookbook: Number Understanding of Language Models and How to Improve It", Haotong Yang, Yi Hu, Shijia Kang, Zhouchen Lin, Muhan Zhang (Peking University). ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2411.03766v3, 5 Mar 2025).

COVERAGE: All 39 pages. About 114,500 of 134,886 chars read in full: main text, limitations, and appendices A.1.7-A.1.8, A.3, A.3.1, A.4.1-A.4.5, A.5. The remaining ~20k chars were the references, skimmed for origins. Appendix pages with only figure axis labels (Figs 5-7, 9-18) were not read as data. Tables 7-9, 12-15 and 17-19 were not read in detail. Appendix A.1.1-A.1.6 and A.2 (prompts) were skimmed only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Frontier LLMs, prompted to output the answer directly with no tools and no CoT, degrade sharply as numbers get longer. Integer addition falls from near-perfect to 15%.
  number: GPT-4o integer add ~100% (1-4 digits), 80% (5-8), ~40% (9-14), 15% (15-20)
  setup: NUPA Test, 1,000 questions per task and length, zero-shot, direct answer, exact match. GPT-4o-2024-08-06.
  quote: "GPT-4o's accuracy drops from nearly 100% in the S range and 80% in the M range to around 40% in the L range and just 15% in the XL range."
  where: p5 (Sec 2.4)
- Claim: Float addition degrades even faster, and fractions and scientific notation are weak even at 1-4 digits.
  number: float add 90% (S), 60% (M), 15% (L), <5% (XL); fractions and sci. notation below 20% even for S
  setup: as above; GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.
  quote: "the accuracy decreases from 90% (S) and 60% (M) to merely 15% (L) and less than 5% (XL)." and "with average accuracy falling below 20%, even for the shortest S-range (1-4 digits)."
  where: p5-6
- Claim: Models cannot reliably locate the i-th digit of a long number. GPT-4o is barely above chance at 61-100 digits.
  number: 20% accuracy vs 10% random baseline
  setup: "get digit" task, XL range (61-100 digits for the 1-100-digit tasks), GPT-4o.
  quote: "In the XL-range, GPT-4o achieves only 20% accuracy, barely above the random guessing 10% baseline"
  where: p6
- Claim: With zero-shot prompting, 5-shot examples add little. They mainly fix output format.
  number: none summarised. Example, Llama-3.1-8B integer add: S 0.95 zero-shot vs 0.94 5-shot; M 0.38 vs 0.41; Qwen2-7B M 0.70 vs 0.82.
  setup: 5-shot, one sample from each of 5 different lengths per task. Table 10.
  quote: "In most tasks, the models can usually produce accurately formatted outputs even in the zero-shot setting, with limited additional benefit observed from few-shot examples, while the few-shot examples can indeed provide some performance improvement."
  where: p21-22 (A.3.1)
- Claim: Tokenizer digit grouping matters for models trained from scratch. One-digit tokenizers beat 2- and 3-digit ones, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Modern LLMs use 3-digit tokens.
  number: none single. Trained on 1-8 digits, tested on D6-D10. The 3B model's 2-digit tokenizer matched 1-digit.
  setup: 0.1B, 0.9B and 3B decoder-only models trained from scratch, one task per model (int add, float add, int multiply). The 3B model trained on 1-40 digits for int add.
  quote: "Tokenizers with an increasing number of digits significantly hinder sub-billion models' NUPA." and "we find no evidence to support the idea that increasing the vocabulary size improves NUPA performance."
  where: p7, p23-24
- Claim: Right-to-left (aligned) segmentation can help. The authors cite Singh & Strouse (2024), not their own test.
  number: none
  quote: "Singh & Strouse (2024) discovers that just alternating the greedy direction from "left-to-right" to "right-to-left" (for integers) can improve performance of Llama-3 and GPT-4."
  where: p7
- Claim: Naive finetuning helps a lot, but the tricks do not transfer to pretrained models. LoRA finetuning Llama-3.1-8B matched or beat GPT-4o on some tasks. Changing PE, tokenizer or format of a trained model hurt.
  number: 800 steps, ~50M samples, 10^5 samples per digit and task. LoRA rank 128, alpha 32.
  setup: Llama-3.1-8B finetuned on a mixed set of all NUPA tasks. Beat or matched GPT-4o on max, max-hard, add-float and truediv. Little gain on digit-understanding tasks.
  quote: "the model's base capacity may not be the main limiting factor, but rather the lack of numerical diversity and task variety in the training data." and "No one can outperform the naive finetuning or the original Llama."
  where: p8-9, A.4.5
- Claim: Rule-following CoT (RF-CoT, the model follows pseudo-code, finetuned) gets near-perfect accuracy within context. It costs far more context and time, and runs out of context quickly on hard tasks.
  number: ~17x slower than a direct answer. 5.625 s/sample vs 0.371 s/sample, batch 128 on an A800. Context limit 2k tokens.
  setup: Llama-3.1-8B finetuned with RF-CoT on a task subset. 3-run average. Table 3 exact match: RF-CoT add-float 5-6 digits 1.00; multiply-fraction 2 digits 0.93, 3 digits 0.88; mod-integer 6 digits 0.67, 7 digits 0.43. GPT-4o on the same: 0.78/0.66, 0.53/0.20, 0.01/0.00.
  quote: "The RF-CoT method is approximately 17 times slower than directly generating the answer" and "with the 2000-token limit, CoT can only handle fraction addition involving numbers up to three digits."
  where: p9-10 (Tables 2-3)
- Claim: Model size stops mattering past a point. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini perform near-identically, as do Qwen2-72B and Qwen2-7B.
  number: none
  quote: "NUPA performance relies more on factors like architecture, training strategies, data diversity, and post-training refinements, rather than simply on increasing model size."
  where: p6
- Claim: "Harder" max (same length, shared prefix) is easier for models than ordinary max. This suggests digit-by-digit comparison and weak use of length information.
  number: none
  quote: "they struggle to effectively use sequence length information, as reflected in their weaker performance on the 'length' tasks in the longer ranges."
  where: p5-6
- Claim: Length hurts both per-digit accuracy and output length, depending on the task. In int add the error is digit match; in max-float it is length (dlength ~30-60 in XL).
  where: p6
- Claim: Reverse formatting and zero padding (pretraining-time formats) are mostly redundant, both helping digit alignment. The "helps carry" explanation is minor.
  number: Table 16, 0.1B, integer add D10 exact match: no pad 0.16±.11; rev 0.69±.11; rev+pad 0.91±.05.
  setup: 0.1B models trained on 1-8 digits, tested at 9-10.
  quote: "The previously believed "helping calculation" function of reverse formatting is minor."
  where: p8, p28
- Claim: Index hints did not help. This contradicts Zhou et al. 2024b, which the authors attribute to model size and digit range (25M, 1-40 digits there).
  where: A.4.4
- Claim: RoPE learns a length shortcut. It wins in-domain on tiny models or little data, but NoPE and Alibi generalise better to longer numbers.
  number: 8-digit digit match, 1.3M model: RoPE 0.091, NoPE 0.061, Alibi 0.056. 0.1B with 1M samples: 0.97, 0.78, 0.23.
  setup: 100M models trained on 1-8 digits, tested on 1-20.
  where: p8, p27 (Table 13)
- Claim: Random (variable-length) tokenization improves out-of-domain length generalization, but is still worse than the one-digit tokenizer.
  where: p7, A.4.2 (Fig 12)

Intro motivating examples, not measured here: "9.11 > 9.9" and "8/7 + 3/5" errors. The authors link them to hallucination in math, reasoning and data-analysis tasks.

LIMITS
- Authors concede (p10): the task list "could still be incomplete and biased toward certain aspects"; few models tested; no solution "fully addresses the problem".
- Tool use is deliberately excluded. The authors do not evaluate calculators or code interpreters, so the paper says nothing for or against PAL or program-aided prompting.
- Prompted CoT is not tested on frontier models. Only a finetuned RF-CoT on an 8B model, with a 2k context cap.
- The tokenizer, PE and format experiments use small models trained from scratch, one task each. They are not tested on frontier models. Models are mostly 2024-era (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1, Qwen2, Mixtral, Llama-2). Reasoning models (o1 etc.) are not tested. Dated for any model after 2024.
- Benchmark numbers are zero-shot direct-answer. The prompts are in A.2, which I did not read.
- Digit-range bins differ by task (S/M/L/XL = 1-4, 5-8, 9-14, 15-20 for hard tasks; 1-10, 11-20, 21-60, 61-100 for easy ones). The bins are not comparable across tasks.
- Few-shot is tested only for format, with 5 examples across lengths.

BUILDS ON: Wei et al. 2022 (CoT); Hu et al. 2024 (RFFT, the rule-following method used for RF-CoT); Lee et al. 2024, Shen et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2024a/b, Cho et al. 2024 (reverse format, zero-padding, index hint); Singh & Strouse 2024 (tokenization direction); Kazemnejad et al. 2023 (NoPE), Press et al. 2022 (Alibi), Su et al. 2024 (RoPE); Sathe et al. 2024, Kudo 2018, Provilkov et al. 2020 (random tokenizer); Hu et al. 2022 (LoRA); Cobbe et al. 2021 (GSM8k).

CODE: RF-CoT prompt format (p29, Appendix A.5.1). A rule is given as Python code, then the model must trace it line by line.
  "Follow the given rule to solve the question.\nRule:\ndef add(num1, num2): ... digit1 = int(num1[-3:]) if num1 else 0 ..."
  The response restates the variable values at every step (e.g. "total = 28 + 35 + 0 = 63").
  This links to the PAL discussion in the note: here the model executes the code in-context rather than an interpreter running it.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p5): performance of GPT-4o, Llama and Qwen models by digit-length range on selected tasks. This is the best single picture of the length cliff.
- Fig 3 (p6): tokenization of 31415.926535897932 under GPT-2, Llama-2 (one-digit), GPT-3.5/4 and Llama-3 (three-digit), and an aligned three-digit tokenizer. This shows how models see numbers. It is a text-and-colour figure and the extraction did not capture its caption, so I cite it from the main text. I cannot confirm the page.
- Fig 4 (p7): 1/2/3-digit tokenizer accuracy curves.
- Fig 1 (p4): exact match, digit match and dlength example.
- Table 3 (p9-10): RF-CoT vs GPT-4o vs finetuned 8B model, exact match by digit count.

NOTE FOR TARGET NOTE (03-core-techniques.md): The note's PAL section already says "don't ask the model to do what code does reliably", and cites the tokens rule in note 01. This paper adds numeric evidence for that rule: the length cliff, digit-lookup failure, and RF-CoT cost. The note currently has no NUPA citation. I read the note only via grep for number/digit/token keywords, so I can't say whether a gap exists elsewhere.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Table 1 and the figure axes extract as mangled text, so plot values (Fig 2, 4) are not recoverable from the text. The figures-captions script did not list Fig 3 (its caption sits in the same text block as the body text). Section 3.4 reads "105 samples" in the extraction, which I interpret as 10^5 (superscript lost). The appendix A.3 summary mentions Tables 7-9 (well-learned digits) that I did not read. The numbers in the Table 16 quote are the ones I verified.
